titleStmt.title: MS. Canon. Class. Lat. 201
MSS. Canon. Class. Lat. (Canonici Latin Classical)

supportDesc.extent: IV, 52 (57), II; two palimpsest front and four palimpsest back end-leaves; two modern fly-leaves of paper on the front and two on the back. Recent foliation 1-57 comprises the parchment back fly-leaves.

binding.p: Plain parchment-covered boards; paper end-leaves impressed with floral designs. The bindings is typical of Jacopo Soranzo’s collection (1686-1761) (see Barker-Benfield, Bookbindings of Canonici manuscripts: a survey of early and non-standard bindings, mostly Italian, in the Canonici collection of the Bodleian Library, University of Oxford, 2020, p. vi).

history.origin: The two units that form the manuscript were produced independently in the same scholastic setting, as proven by the presence of the same hand on both units. The aspect of the units, including their quire arrangements, layout, and decoration, suggests that they were unlikely to have been prepared as parts of the same manuscript (see descriptions of Unit I and II). Indeed they also seem to have been used independently.
history.provenance: In the fifteenth century the manuscript possibly in its current form entered the library of Marco and Leonardo Giustiniani in Venice, as proven by the note of possession on fol. 57v, “Marci et Leonardi Iustiniani hic liber est”, and “Leonardi Iustiniani est codex iste” on fol. IIIv

The manuscript then entered Jacopo Soranzo’s collection (Alessio, 'Brunetto Latini e Cicerone (e i dettatori)', in G. Alessio, Lucidissima dictandi peritia. Studi di grammatica e retorica Medievale, F. Bolognini (ed.), Venice, 2015, p. 14) even though no shelf-mark remains. Identified by J. B. Mitchell (card catalogue, Bodleian Library) as 289 in quarto in Soranzo's catalogue.

msIdentifier.idno: MS. Canon. Class. Lat. 201, Unit I, fols. 1-8

msItem.title: Commentary on Cicero, De inventione I
msItem.note: Ed. G. Alessio, 'Brunetto Latini e Cicerone (e i dettatori)', pp. 19-76. This is the only known manuscript, imperfect at end due to loss of leaves after fol. 8.

According to Alessio, the commentary was written by an Italian author drawing on French masters, particularly Manegold of Lautenbach and William of Champeaux. The Italian origin of the master would be supported by the reference to Milan’s defeat by Cremona as a recent event. On this basis, Alessio suggests a date between 1110 and 1137 for the composition of the text, also seeing a possible link of this master with the school of Thierry of Chartres (Alessio, 'Brunetto Latini e Cicerone (e i dettatori)'; J. O. Ward, 'The Date of the Commentary on Cicero’s De inventione by Thierry of Chartres (ca. 1095-1160?) and the Cornifician Attack on the Liberal Arts', Viator, 3. 1 (1972), pp. 245-247).

The commentary appears to have been used by Brunetto Latini in his Rettorica. He might have encountered a copy of the commentary in France, as he began writing the Rettorica during his exile in France between 1260 and 1266, following the Ghibelline victory at the Battle of Montaperti; documents place him in Arras and Paris in 1263, and in Bar-sur-Aube in 1264 (see B. Ceva, Brunetto Latini l’uomo e l’opera, Milan, 1965). This suggests that the commentary itself circulated in France in the thirteenth century.

layoutDesc.layout: Ruled with hard point for 2 columns of 42 lines, written space 9 [181] 22 9 [51 (8) 53] 21 (fol. 4). Written above top line.

handDesc.handNote: One hand in a mature Caroline minuscule, probably of French origin. The same hand recurs less compressed and abbreviated in Unit II.

origin.origDate: first half of the twelfth century

history.provenance: The unit presents damage on the external pages. Unit I is also imperfect, indicating an individual circulation, possibly without proper binding.

msIdentifier.idno: MS. Canon. Class. Lat. 201, Unit II, fols. 9-52

supportDesc.foliation: The unit displays an independent 15th-century foliation 1-44.
supportDesc.collation: 1-58 (9-16; 17-24; 25-32; 33-40; 41-48); 64 (49-52); later mediaeval catchwords on q. 15; quire signature III and IIII on quires 3 and 4.

layoutDesc.layout: 34 long lines, written above top line. Written space (fol. 40) 19 [155] 38 11 [104] 27 (f. 40).

handDesc.handNote: The unit is copied by the same as Unit I, in a mature Caroline minuscule. The script is more regular, less compress and less abbreviated than in Unit I. Titles in a mixed alphabet of uncial and capital letters, by the same scribe.

Several marginal notes by two 15th-century northern-Italian humanistic hands, one of which is also responsible for the note of possession on fol. 57v, while the other writes the note of possession on fol. IIIv. Both hands display all the characteristics of the northern littera antiqua: cursive aspect, use or a cursive round r, straight s at the end of the words sloping to the right (S. Zamponi, 'La scrittura umanistica', in T. De Robertis, N. Giovè (eds), Le ragioni della scrittura. Piccoli scritti di paleografia, Rome, 2021, pp. 113-126: 119-121). Comparison against one of Leonardo Giustinian’s autograph manuscripts, Firenze, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Redi 118, indicates that neither hand of the marginal notes is that of Leonardo. The hand of the note on fol. 57v shows similarities with that of Sebastiano Borsa, a copyist and notary with a humanistic training, who was active in the first decades of the fifteenth century and was also involved in Leonardo Giustinian’s humanistic circle (E. Barile, Littera antiqua e scritture alla greca, Venezia, 1994, p. 18-32). It is possible that the hand belonged to Marco, Leonardo Giustinian’s younger brother of, who is also known to have studied rhetoric and grammar and is as well mentioned in the notes on f. 57v.

decoDesc.decoNote: A zoomorphic initial (“S”) in the shape of an eagle on f. 9r. The style of the illumination points to northern France, and particularly to the Norman ornamental tradition. In the illustration of the wings and feathers of the bird we can see a parallel with the representation of the animal, found for instance in the initial (“Q”) of an eleventh-century codex of Avranches (Bibliothèque Municipale, MS 97, f. 240v). The position of the claws and neck can be compared with those of another later French manuscript, Anger, Bibliothèque Municipale 243. Not in Pächt and Alexander.

origin.origDate: first half of the twelfth century

history.provenance: As proven by the quire-signatures, the manuscript was planned as distinct unit. There is separate foliation and Unit II was read and annotated independently of Unit I during the fifteenth century, when the manuscript belonged to the library of the Giustinian family. Both Marco and Leonardo Giustinian received a humanistic education, cultivated humanistic interests and collected a library of Latin and Greek classics (which has yet to be reconstructed; G. Folena, 'La cultura volgare e l’Umanesimo cavalleresco nel Veneto', in Umanesimo europeo e umanesimo veneziano, ed. V. Branca, Firenze, 1963, p. 156). They may therefore have had a direct interest in this manuscript.
